[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the East Asian Social Survey (EASS) or World Values Survey (WVS) for Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan, measuring community reciprocity, social trust, and subjective well-being over 10+ years — Allows testing whether high reciprocity reverses the typical positive association between trust/cohesion indicators (HDI, GPI) and well-being, by modeling interaction effects in multilevel regression.

[PATH:theoretical] Ethnographic or experimental studies on 'reciprocity burden' in collectivist communities (e.g., rural China or urban South Korea) where strong reciprocity norms impose social obligations that reduce well-being despite high cohesion — Provides qualitative evidence and theoretical mechanisms (e.g., social pressure, inequality in reciprocity) explaining the hypothesized negative moderation, which can be formalized into testable models.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative analysis using the OECD Regional Well-Being dataset combined with community-level reciprocity indices (e.g., from the East Asian Community Survey) to examine cross-regional variation in the reciprocity-cohesion-wellbeing link — Enables detection of whether the reversal effect is specific to high-reciprocity, high-inequality East Asian contexts versus low-reciprocity ones, addressing scope conditions.

scope.domain: East Asian societies with strong collectivist norms and high income inequality

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of Japanese General Social Survey (JGSS) and Korean General Social Survey (KGSS) waves (2000-2020) linking community reciprocity indices to subjective well-being and regional HDI/GPI — These repeated cross-sectional surveys contain items on social trust, reciprocity norms, and life satisfaction, allowing direct testing of the hypothesized positive relationship across time and within collectivist contexts.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case study of Chinese urban neighborhoods using the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) to construct reciprocity metrics and correlate them with subjective well-being and community-level HDI — CFPS provides panel data on social interactions, trust, and well-being; analyzing within-community reciprocity can isolate the effect from individual-level confounds and test the scope condition.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published studies on social capital and well-being in East Asia, focusing on reciprocity as a distinct dimension from general trust — Existing literature often conflates reciprocity with trust; a targeted meta-analysis can disaggregate effects and assess whether reciprocity metrics uniquely enhance the cohesion-wellbeing link in collectivist societies.

[PATH:empirical] Re-analysis of World Values Survey (WVS) and East Asian Social Survey (EASS) data, focusing on rural older adults in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan, with reciprocity indices (e.g., gift-giving frequency, mutual aid networks) included as moderators in regression models predicting subjective well-being. — Directly tests the negative association between HDI/GPI social cohesion/trust indicators and subjective well-being when reciprocity is accounted for, using cross-national panel data that includes collectivist subpopulations.

[PATH:literature] Qualitative meta-ethnography of ethnographic studies on reciprocity norms and well-being in East Asian rural communities (e.g., studies on 'guanxi' in China, 'kankei' in Japan, 'cheon' in Korea). — Provides contextual understanding of how reciprocity obligations may invert the expected positive relationship between social trust and well-being, supporting or refuting the hypothesized negative association.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling paper on 'social cohesion as a burden' in collectivist cultures, drawing on social exchange theory and the concept of 'relational costs' (e.g., work by Markus & Kitayama or Uchida et al.). — Offers a causal framework to explain why high trust and cohesion might reduce well-being when reciprocity is mandatory, providing testable predictions for the observed negative association.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey data from the World Values Survey (WVS) and East Asian Social Survey (EASS) for urban, younger cohorts in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Chinese cities (2010-2023), analyzing subpopulation responses to individualistic value items (e.g., Schwartz values) and correlating with subjective well-being (SWB) scales, while controlling for social cohesion and trust indicators from HDI and GPI datasets but omitting reciprocity metrics. — Directly tests the hypothesis by isolating the effect of social cohesion/trust on SWB among individualistic subpopulations, with reciprocity excluded, using existing panel data to confirm or refute the negative influence.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies using vignette-based surveys or behavioral games (e.g., trust games, public goods games) in urban East Asian settings, measuring SWB responses to manipulated social trust and cohesion scenarios, while deliberately not measuring reciprocity, to isolate causal direction. — Provides causal inference by controlling for reciprocity omission, addressing the disputed status and moderate confidence through controlled manipulation rather than observational correlation.

[PATH:theoretical] Critical review of cultural psychology literature on the 'dark side' of social cohesion in individualistic contexts, such as studies on social pressure, conformity costs, and autonomy-threat in tight-knit East Asian urban communities (e.g., Yamagishi, 1988; Markus & Kitayama, 1991), synthesizing theoretical frameworks that predict negative SWB effects when reciprocity norms are absent. — Offers theoretical grounding for the hypothesized negative relationship, explaining why excluding reciprocity might turn trust/cohesion into a burden for individualistic subpopulations, and suggests mechanisms to test empirically.
